def: likely to cause resentment or hurt feelings, especially by making unfair comparisons between people
ex: Ranking the volunteers by hours worked put the manager in an invidious position with her team.
Priya refused to make invidious comparisons between her two children's report cards.

cloze.s: Choosing just one of three equally deserving nurses for the award was an ___ task that was sure to hurt feelings.

note: Formal; common in 'invidious comparison' and 'invidious position.' Not the same as insidious (harmful in a gradual, hidden way).

def: deliberately disloyal and deceitful; ready to betray people who trust you
ex: The novel's perfidious advisor smiles at the queen while secretly plotting with her enemies.
Fans called the star's sudden move to their rival a perfidious betrayal of the city.

cloze.s: The ___ business partner secretly sold their client list to a competitor while swearing he was loyal.

note: Formal and strongly negative.

def: showing eager, attentive concern for someone's comfort, health or well-being
ex: The nurse was solicitous of Mr. Okafor, checking on his pain every hour through the night.
Our host was so solicitous that she refilled our glasses before we noticed they were empty.

cloze.s: After Diego's surgery, his ___ neighbors brought meals daily and kept asking whether he needed anything else.

note: Often followed by 'of' or 'about'; can hint at attention that is a little excessive.

def: sweet, soft and pleasant to hear
ex: The dulcet sound of a flute floated across the quiet garden party.
Wei teased his roommate, who woke everyone at dawn with the dulcet tones of a blaring alarm.

cloze.s: The harpist's ___ melody was so soft and sweet that the baby fell asleep within minutes.

note: Often used ironically, as in 'the dulcet tones of' something loud or unpleasant.

def: happening by lucky chance at exactly the right moment, as if arranged by fate
ex: A providential break in the storm let the hikers reach the shelter safely.
Running into an old classmate who worked at the bank proved providential for Aisha's loan application.

cloze.s: The ___ arrival of an off-duty doctor at the scene of the crash saved the cyclist's life.

also: relating to divine providence, God's care and guidance

def: ridiculously old-fashioned or outdated; literally, from the time before the biblical Flood
ex: The office still runs on an antediluvian computer system that crashes every afternoon.
Sofia rolled her eyes at her uncle's antediluvian ideas about who should cook dinner.

cloze.s: The museum's ___ fax machine, older than most of its staff, finally broke down for good.

note: Usually humorous or mocking. From Latin for 'before the flood.'

def: so unhappy or disappointed that nothing can comfort or cheer you
ex: The disconsolate fans sat in silence long after the final whistle.
Malik was disconsolate for days after his dog ran away.

cloze.s: After missing the deadline by a single day, Hannah sat ___ at her desk, refusing every attempt to cheer her up.

def: full of bitter, long-lasting resentment or hostility
ex: The divorce became rancorous once the couple began fighting over the house.
After a rancorous debate, the town council voted to close the public pool.

cloze.s: Years of ___ feuding over a property line left the two families unable to share a single holiday.

def: too eager to give orders or unwanted help; bossy and interfering, especially about small matters
ex: An officious security guard insisted on checking every bag twice, even the empty ones.
Olga found her officious coworker exhausting, since he corrected everyone's emails without being asked.

cloze.s: The ___ hall monitor scolded students for walking too slowly and reported them for every tiny rule breach.

note: Not the same as 'official.' Negative: describes someone who overuses a little authority.

def: insisting on immediate obedience in a curt, rude way that allows no discussion
ex: The manager's peremptory email simply said, 'Be in my office at nine.'
Tomás bristled at the peremptory tone the clerk used with elderly customers.

cloze.s: With a ___ wave of her hand, the director dismissed the question and ordered everyone back to work.

also: in law, final and not open to challenge, as in a 'peremptory challenge' of a juror

def: joking about sex or bodily functions in a crude but playful, humorous way
ex: The comedian's ribald jokes made some guests laugh and others blush.
Old sailors' songs are full of ribald verses about life ashore.

cloze.s: Grandma was shocked when the best man's toast turned ___, full of crude, cheeky jokes about the honeymoon.

def: calm and unemotional by temperament; not easily excited, upset or stirred to action
ex: Jamal's phlegmatic manner made him a steady presence in the chaotic newsroom.
Even when the flight was canceled, the phlegmatic traveler simply opened a book and waited.

cloze.s: Unlike his excitable brother, the ___ Kwame rarely showed strong feelings of any kind, even at weddings.

note: Neutral or mildly negative (can suggest dullness). Comes from the old medical theory of four 'humors,' one being phlegm.

def: staying calm and in control even during a crisis or under great pressure
ex: The unflappable pilot calmly guided the plane through heavy turbulence.
As a teacher, Fatima is unflappable, no matter how loud the class gets.

cloze.s: Even when the stage lights failed mid-speech, the ___ host kept talking as if nothing had happened.

note: Informal and positive; from 'flap,' meaning a state of panic.

def: only just beginning to form, so not yet fully developed, clear or organized
ex: Priya had an inchoate idea for a business but no real plan yet.
The protest movement was still inchoate, with no leaders or clear demands.

cloze.s: His thoughts about the novel were still ___, a jumble of images without a plot or main characters.

note: Pronounced in-KOH-it. Comes from Latin for 'begin,' not from 'chaos.'

def: so closely linked or tangled together that the parts cannot be separated
ex: For Kwame, music and memory are inextricable; every song recalls a moment from his past.
The city's history is inextricable from the river that runs through it.

cloze.s: Money worries and health problems had become ___ for the family, so fixing one without the other was impossible.

def: not telling the truth; habitually lying or deliberately false
ex: The company's mendacious ads claimed the drink could cure the common cold.
Reporters exposed the mendacious claims in the official statement within hours.

cloze.s: The witness's ___ testimony fell apart when security footage showed she had been home all night.

def: highly relevant and well suited to the situation or topic being discussed
ex: Liam opened his speech with an apposite quote about courage.
The lawyer's apposite question exposed the gap in the witness's story.

cloze.s: Her remark about the dangers of overconfidence was especially ___, given that the team had just lost to the last-place side.

note: Formal. Not the same as 'opposite.'

def: having an extreme, selfish desire for money or possessions
ex: The avaricious landlord raised the rent every year while ignoring repairs.
In the old story, an avaricious king wished that everything he touched would turn to gold.

cloze.s: The ___ collector bought every rare coin he could find, never satisfied with what he already owned.

def: completely clear and transparent, like still, clean water
ex: We could see fish darting over the sand in the limpid lagoon.
The pond was so limpid that every pebble on the bottom was visible.

cloze.s: Yuki snorkeled in the ___ mountain lake, where the water was as clear as glass.

also: of writing or style: clear and easy to understand

def: talking easily, quickly and at length; very talkative
ex: Our voluble tour guide kept up a stream of stories for three hours.
Usually voluble, Hannah went oddly quiet when asked about her new job.

cloze.s: The ___ salesman talked nonstop through the entire test drive, barely pausing to breathe.

def: excessively flattering and smoothly polite in a way that seems fake and self-serving
ex: The unctuous waiter praised every single order as 'an excellent choice.'
Guests grew tired of the host's unctuous smile and endless empty compliments.

cloze.s: The ___ realtor gushed over every room, calling a cramped closet 'charming,' which made us trust him less.

note: Strongly negative. Its literal meaning is 'oily or greasy.'

def: looking or sounding sad and gloomy, often in an exaggerated way
ex: The basset hound gazed up at us with its lugubrious, droopy eyes.
The band's lugubrious ballads made the birthday party feel like a funeral.

cloze.s: The old movie's slow, ___ theme music had half the audience feeling gloomy before the opening scene ended.

def: grossly unfair and morally wrong, especially in a way that harms the weak
ex: Critics called the tax that fell hardest on the poorest families iniquitous.
The report described iniquitous working conditions inside the factory.

cloze.s: Charging desperate patients ten times the normal price for basic medicine was an ___ practice.

def: stubbornly refusing to change your mind or behavior, despite argument or persuasion
ex: Despite every appeal, the obdurate official refused to reopen the case.
Diego remained obdurate, insisting the restaurant had gotten his order wrong.

cloze.s: No matter how many engineers explained the risks, the ___ owner would not delay the bridge's opening.

def: eager to argue or fight; aggressively defiant
ex: The truculent customer was shouting at staff before the manager even arrived.
Teenagers can turn truculent when they feel they are being treated unfairly.

cloze.s: When the referee warned him, the ___ player squared up as if he wanted to fight the official too.

def: in keeping with good taste and proper behavior; dignified and polite
ex: The wedding guests remained decorous until the dancing started.
Students were asked to keep a decorous silence during the ceremony.

cloze.s: Even at the noisy family reunion, Grandma Sofia expected a ___ dinner, with napkins on laps and no shouting.

def: deliberately one-sided, presenting a biased view in order to promote a particular cause or opinion
ex: The documentary was so tendentious that it ignored every expert who disagreed.
Reviewers criticized the history book as tendentious for cherry-picking its evidence.

cloze.s: The pamphlet's ___ summary of the study left out every finding that weakened its argument.

note: Not the same as 'tenuous' (weak or flimsy).

def: so light, delicate and thin that you can almost see through it, usually of fabric
ex: The dancer wore a diaphanous scarf that fluttered as she spun across the stage.
Diaphanous curtains let soft morning light fill the bedroom.

cloze.s: A ___ veil of fine silk floated over the bride's face without hiding her smile.

def: severely critical of others; quick to find fault and disapprove
ex: A censorious neighbor complained about every paint color on the street.
Maria worried that her censorious mother-in-law would criticize the holiday dinner.

cloze.s: The ___ critic found fault with nearly every film he reviewed and rarely gave more than one star.

note: Related to 'censor,' but means harshly critical, not banning things.

def: behaving as if you are better than others; haughty and scornful
ex: The sommelier gave a supercilious smile when Liam asked for ice in his wine.
Her supercilious tone made the new interns afraid to ask questions.

cloze.s: Raising one eyebrow, the ___ clerk looked down at our muddy boots as if we were beneath his notice.

def: sentimental in an exaggerated, sugary way that feels false or embarrassing
ex: The movie's mawkish ending, with swelling violins and tearful hugs, made critics groan.
Kwame avoided mawkish greeting cards and wrote his own simple note instead.

cloze.s: The ad was so ___, with slow-motion puppies and syrupy music, that viewers found it more cringeworthy than moving.

def: innocent, open and trusting, sometimes too much so; lacking cunning or worldly experience
ex: Her ingenuous question about who pays for the free samples made the whole room laugh.
Aisha had an ingenuous faith that everyone at her new job wanted to help her.

cloze.s: The ___ young tourist believed the stranger's story and handed over his wallet for 'safekeeping.'

note: Not 'ingenious' (clever). Its opposite, 'disingenuous,' means insincere.

def: too large, strong or difficult to be overcome
ex: Lack of funding proved an insuperable obstacle for the small museum.
To the exhausted team, a ten-goal deficit seemed insuperable.

cloze.s: Without roads or bridges, the jagged mountains posed an ___ barrier to the invading army.

def: showing far too much confidence or pride; excessively arrogant or presumptuous
ex: His overweening ambition eventually cost him every friendship he had.
Analysts blamed the company's collapse on its overweening confidence in a single product.

cloze.s: Her ___ pride made her ignore all advice, certain she could win the marathon without ever training.

note: Usually before 'ambition,' 'pride' or 'confidence.'

def: minor and easily forgiven; not seriously wrong
ex: Forgetting to return a borrowed pen is a venial offense, not a betrayal.
The editor overlooked venial slips in style but never factual errors.

cloze.s: Compared with stealing the money, his habit of arriving five minutes late was a ___ fault.

note: In Catholic teaching, a venial sin is less serious than a mortal sin. Don't confuse with 'venal' (open to bribery).

def: producing many offspring, crops or new ideas; highly fertile or productive
ex: The fecund river valley grew enough grain to feed the entire region.
Wei's fecund imagination produced a new story idea almost every week.

cloze.s: Rabbits are famously ___, with a single pair able to produce dozens of young in one year.

def: easily irritated and bad-tempered; cranky and grumpy
ex: The crotchety cat hissed at anyone who sat in its favorite chair.
Malik gets crotchety when he hasn't had his morning coffee.

cloze.s: Short on sleep after the overnight flight, Priya was ___ all day, snapping at anyone who spoke to her.

note: Informal; often used of older people, but fits anyone in a grumpy mood.

def: done carelessly, without enough attention to detail or quality
ex: The slipshod repair job left water leaking under the sink within a week.
The teacher would not accept slipshod essays full of spelling errors.

cloze.s: Inspectors blamed the collapse on ___ construction, with missing bolts and badly mixed concrete.

def: so ridiculous or poor that it deserves to be laughed at
ex: The team's risible defense allowed six goals in the first half alone.
Tomás called the offer of a one-dollar raise risible and walked out of the meeting.

cloze.s: The thief's excuse, that the TV had somehow fallen into his car by accident, was frankly ___.

note: Usually scornful.

def: extremely bad or unpleasant; of terrible quality
ex: The hotel's food was execrable, so we ate at the diner every night.
Olga apologized for her execrable handwriting on the birthday card.

cloze.s: The coffee at the bus station was ___: bitter, burnt and served lukewarm in a leaky cup.

def: extremely badly; to a terribly low standard or degree
ex: The team played abysmally and lost by thirty points.
Wages at the old factory were abysmally low, even for the region.

cloze.s: The new restaurant was so ___ run that orders took two hours and half of them were wrong.

def: in a gradual, hidden way that causes harm before anyone notices
ex: Mold had spread insidiously behind the walls for years before anyone noticed the smell.
Chronic stress can insidiously damage health over many years.

cloze.s: High blood pressure works ___, causing serious damage for years without obvious symptoms.

def: in a smooth, easy way that sounds too quick or shallow to be sincere or well thought out
ex: The spokesperson glibly promised the problem would be fixed by Friday.
It's easy to glibly tell someone to 'just relax' when you aren't the one worrying.

cloze.s: He answered the tough question ___, with a quick joke that showed he hadn't really thought about it.

def: in a joking, not serious way, often about a serious matter when humor may be inappropriate
ex: Jamal facetiously suggested selling his car to pay for one fancy dinner.
She was speaking facetiously, but her boss took the comment literally.

cloze.s: When asked how the exam went, Yuki ___ replied that she had probably invented a new branch of math.

def: in a grimly mocking or cynical way, as if scornfully amused
ex: 'Great, another meeting about meetings,' Liam said sardonically.
The critic smiled sardonically as the actor forgot his lines yet again.

cloze.s: Stuck in traffic for the third hour, Maria ___ remarked that at least they would get to see the sunrise.

def: without showing any emotion or reaction on your face or in your manner
ex: The judge listened impassively as the verdict was read aloud.
The palace guard stared impassively ahead while tourists tried to make him laugh.

cloze.s: Even as the crowd booed, the umpire stood ___, his face showing no reaction at all.

def: in a way that suggests someone or something is unimportant or of little value
ex: He spoke disparagingly about his old job, calling it pointless busywork.
Critics referred disparagingly to the new building as 'the shoebox.'

cloze.s: Instead of praising her assistant's report, Hannah's boss spoke ___ of it, calling it 'adequate at best.'

def: always accurately and without making a single mistake
ex: The archer hit the target unerringly, arrow after arrow.
Kwame unerringly picks the best dish on any menu.

cloze.s: Many migrating birds find their way ___ back to the same nesting grounds every spring.

def: in a humiliating and shameful way that damages one's reputation
ex: The defending champions were ignominiously knocked out in the first round.
The scheme ended ignominiously, with its founder fleeing the country.

cloze.s: After weeks of boasting, the race favorite tripped at the start and ___ finished last.

def: in a way that shows puzzlement or mild amusement, as if asking a question
ex: The puppy tilted its head quizzically at the squeaking toy.
Sofia raised an eyebrow quizzically when I said I'd bought a boat.

cloze.s: Unsure what the strange phrase meant, Diego looked ___ at his teacher and waited for an explanation.

def: in a fiercely and bitterly critical way
ex: The review scathingly described the musical as 'two hours I will never get back.'
Fatima wrote scathingly about the hospital's long wait times.

cloze.s: The judge spoke ___ of the company's conduct, calling it reckless, dishonest and cruel.

def: with great energy, strength and enthusiasm; heartily
ex: The fans sang lustily as their team ran onto the field.
The newborn cried lustily, to the relief of the delivery team.

cloze.s: Everyone at the table joined in ___ for 'Happy Birthday,' singing loudly enough to be heard outside.

note: Despite the link to 'lust,' it usually describes hearty singing, cheering, crying or eating.

def: to be necessary, proper or in someone's interest to do something
ex: It behooves travelers to check the visa rules before booking any flights.
It would behoove the team to practice free throws before the playoffs.

cloze.s: With exams next week, it would ___ you to start reviewing your notes tonight.

note: Almost always used with 'it': 'It behooves you to...' The British spelling is 'behove.'

def: to relax and take great pleasure in something comfortable or enjoyable
ex: After the long hike, Aisha luxuriated in a hot bath with a good book.
The cat luxuriated in a warm patch of afternoon sun.

cloze.s: On the first day of vacation, Liam planned to ___ in the hotel spa for hours.

note: Followed by 'in.' Not the same as 'luxuriant' (lush and abundant).

def: to require something to be true or to exist beforehand; to assume in advance
ex: The plan presupposes that everyone will arrive on time.
Advanced classes presuppose some knowledge of basic algebra.

cloze.s: The recipe's instructions ___ that you already own a stand mixer, which many readers don't.

def: to formally cancel or repeal a law, agreement or right
ex: The new government abrogated the trade treaty within a month.
Workers argued the policy abrogated their long-standing right to overtime pay.

cloze.s: The two countries agreed to ___ the old treaty and negotiate a new one from scratch.

note: Formal. Don't confuse with 'arrogate' (to claim something without the right).

def: to leave secretly and quickly, often to avoid arrest or while taking money
ex: The club's treasurer absconded with all of its savings.
The suspect absconded days before his trial date.

cloze.s: The bookkeeper ___ with two million dollars and was later found living abroad under a false name.

note: Often 'abscond with' money or valuables.

def: to cheat someone, especially by taking their money or not paying what you owe
ex: The scammers bilked retirees out of their savings with fake investments.
A contractor bilked dozens of homeowners by taking deposits and never starting work.

cloze.s: The fake charity ___ donors out of millions before investigators shut it down.

note: Usually 'bilk someone out of' money.

def: to lecture someone at length in a loud, aggressive or critical way
ex: The coach harangued the players for twenty minutes after the loss.
A passenger harangued the driver about the late bus all the way downtown.

cloze.s: Instead of listening, the angry customer ___ the cashier for ten minutes about the store's prices.

note: Also a noun: a long, loud, angry speech.

def: to overwhelm with more of something than can easily be handled
ex: The office was inundated with complaints after the price increase.
After the viral video, the small bakery was inundated with orders.

cloze.s: After her phone number was posted online by mistake, Olga was ___ with calls from strangers.

also: to flood an area with water
